title: Practical Work and Project Work
tagline: Paper II: the practical exercises, field techniques and project requirements that carry 30 marks alongside the theory paper.

overview.intro: Paper II assesses the practical side of the subject, and it is where the theory is used rather than recited. This unit covers the prescribed practical work: measuring distance and direction, interpreting and marking maps, recording weather observations, working with diagrams and cross-sections, and carrying out a small field study. It then sets out how a geography project is planned, executed and presented, and the conventions that keep a practical record accurate and reproducible. The 30 marks at stake make this as examinable as any theory chapter.

learningOutcomes: Carry out the prescribed measurements of distance, height and direction.
Interpret and annotate maps and construct a cross-section.
Record and present weather observations correctly.
Plan and execute a geography project with a stated method.
Present practical work in a form that another person could reproduce.

learn.title: Measurement of distance, height and direction

blocks.text: Practical measurement begins with distance, which on a map is converted from map length using the scale, and on the ground is measured with a measuring tape, a rod and eye, or by pacing with a known stride length. Height is obtained from contour values, from a spot height, or in the field by an aneroid barometer whose reading is corrected against a known point. Direction is measured as a bearing from north using a prismatic compass, and the bearing is recorded as a three-figure azimuth so that 045 degrees cannot be confused with 45 degrees in a note.

blocks.caption: Methods of practical measurement
rows: Measuring tape, pacing, or rod and eye
Scaled with a ruler against the bar or representative fraction
Aneroid barometer corrected at a known point
Clinometer reading, or rise over run
Height difference divided by scaled ground distance
Grid or true north with declination corrected

items: Always state the instrument and the date, since readings drift with conditions.
Take repeat readings and note the average rather than trusting one observation.
Record the unit with every figure: metres, millibars, degrees or kilometres.
Check that the direction is taken from the printed north, not the page edge.

blocks.text: A weather record requires regular observations at stated times, normally at 08:30, 14:30 and 20:30, using instruments kept in a shaded, ventilated Stevenson screen. The elements recorded are temperature, both dry and wet bulb for humidity, atmospheric pressure from a barometer, rainfall measured in a rain gauge to 0.1 millimetres, wind speed and direction from an anemometer and a vane, and cloud amount and type estimated in eighths of the sky. Each entry carries the time and the instrument used.

Presenting the record is part of the exercise. Temperature and pressure are plotted on a line graph with time on the horizontal axis and two vertical scales, rainfall is shown as bars, and wind is indicated by arrows whose length encodes speed. Humidity may be plotted from the wet and dry bulb difference using a hygrometric table. A full weather record should include a summary of the range of each element and a short interpretation of the pattern, for example noting that pressure fell before rain arrived.

blocks.caption: Instruments and the element each measures
rows: Degrees Celsius, read at stated times
Derived from the difference using a table
Millibars, corrected to a known elevation
Direction in degrees, speed in km/h

items.text: Rainfall collected in a standard gauge and measured in a measuring cylinder.
items.note: The reading is taken as 0.1 mm of rainfall, and the date of emptying is recorded.

items.text: A drop in pressure recorded over 24 hours before a shower.
items.note: An interpretation entry showing the student reads the pattern rather than only the numbers.

blocks.text: Practical map work involves both reading and marking. Reading a map means extracting information: the direction of flow of a river from its V-shaped contours, the nature of the slope from contour spacing, the transport network from symbols, and the relationship between settlement and relief. Marking a map means transferring information accurately onto a copy, using the conventional symbols, keeping the positions exact and labelling each feature.

A cross-section is drawn by laying a strip of paper along the required line on the map, pricking through each contour and the points of interest, marking the height of each on a prepared vertical scale, and joining the marks with a smooth line that shows the profile of the land. The vertical scale is usually exaggerated relative to the horizontal scale so that relief is visible, and both scales must be stated on the finished figure, together with the direction of the section.

items: Take the section line across the landform rather than along it, so the shape shows.
State the vertical exaggeration, since an unstated exaggeration misleads.
Label the start and end points and show the horizontal scale below the profile.
Mark features such as the river, road or settlement where they cross the line.
Keep the pencil light for construction lines and firm for the finished profile.

learn.title: Planning and presenting a geography project

blocks.text: A project is a sustained investigation of a defined question, and its marks come from method as much as from findings. It begins by stating a clear aim and a hypothesis that can be tested, for example that the northern slope of the valley carries denser settlement because it is sheltered. The method must then be stated fully: where observations were made, when, with what instrument, how many samples were taken and how the data was recorded. Analysis follows, using tables, simple statistics, maps and graphs, and the conclusion must answer the original question directly and state the limitations of the work.

blocks.caption: Structure of a geography project
rows: The question being investigated, stated in one sentence
Location, dates, instruments, sample size and recording technique
Tables and observations exactly as recorded, with units
Maps, graphs, simple averages and comparison against the hypothesis
Direct answer to the aim, supported by the data
Errors and constraints that could affect the result
Questionnaires, sketch maps and raw readings

blocks.text: Presentation rules are simple and strictly marked: number every page, give every table and figure a title and a number, state units with every figure, keep the handwriting legible, and cite the source of any data that was not observed personally. A project that copies figures without a source, or that reaches a conclusion its own data does not support, loses heavily.

items.text: A survey of shop types along a street transect.
items.note: Method states the length walked, the interval at which each shop was recorded and the classification used.

items.text: A river measurement at three points showing velocity falling downstream.
items.note: Data in a table with distance, depth and velocity, followed by a graph and a conclusion about gradient.

keyPoints: Paper II carries 30 marks alongside the 70 marks of the theory paper.
Distance on a map is converted by the scale; on the ground by tape, pacing or rod and eye.
Height comes from contours, spot heights or a corrected aneroid barometer.
Direction is measured as a three-figure bearing from the printed north.
Weather observations need fixed times and instruments kept in a shaded, ventilated screen.
Rainfall is recorded to 0.1 millimetres and wind direction in degrees.
A cross-section exaggerates the vertical scale, which must be stated on the figure.
A project states an aim, a hypothesis, a method, data, analysis, findings and limitations.
Every table and figure needs a number, a title and units.
Uncited figures and unsupported conclusions lose marks heavily.
examFocus: Practical answers are marked on procedure, so state the instrument, the timing and the unit for every measurement.
In cross-section questions, remember to declare the vertical exaggeration and both scales.
Project questions reward a stated hypothesis and a limitations section, which weaker candidates omit.

questions.prompt: Weather instruments are housed in a Stevenson screen because it:
options: Keeps them in shade with free ventilation
questions.answer: Keeps them in shade with free ventilation
questions.explanation: Standard conditions require shade to prevent radiation error and free ventilation so the air around the instruments reflects true air conditions.

questions.prompt: A bearing is written as 045 rather than 45 in order to:
options: Avoid confusion with other values and keep three figures
questions.answer: Avoid confusion with other values and keep three figures
questions.explanation: The three-figure convention standardises the notation so that a bearing such as 005 is not misread as 5 or 50.

questions.prompt: In a contour cross-section, the vertical scale is usually exaggerated so that:
options: Relief is visible on the drawing
questions.answer: Relief is visible on the drawing
questions.explanation: Horizontal distances greatly exceed vertical relief, so without exaggeration a real profile would look almost flat.

questions.prompt: Paper II of the ISC Class XI Geography examination carries:
options: 30 marks of practical and project work
questions.answer: 30 marks of practical and project work
questions.explanation: The subject is examined through Paper I Theory of 70 marks and Paper II Practical Work and Project Work of 30 marks.

questions.prompt: The instrument used to measure rainfall, reading to 0.1 millimetres, is the rain __________ .
questions.explanation: The gauge collects rainfall and the amount is measured in a graduated cylinder, with the date of emptying recorded.

questions.prompt: A testable statement that a geography project sets out to confirm or reject is called a __________ .
questions.explanation: The hypothesis gives the investigation direction, and the findings are then stated as supporting or failing to support it.

questions.prompt: State four elements that should be recorded in a weather observation.
questions.answer: Four elements are temperature in degrees Celsius from a maximum and minimum thermometer; atmospheric pressure in millibars from a barometer; rainfall in millimetres to one decimal place from a rain gauge; and wind direction in degrees together with wind speed in kilometres per hour from a vane and anemometer. Humidity derived from dry and wet bulb readings is also accepted.
questions.explanation: Each element needs its instrument and unit, since the record is marked on correct notation as well as content.

questions.prompt: Describe how a contour cross-section is drawn.
questions.answer: Lay a strip of paper along the required section line on the map, marking the two end points and the direction. Prick through every point where a contour crosses the strip and mark any feature such as a river, road or settlement. Transfer the strip to a prepared diagram, aligning it with the horizontal scale, and mark the height of each pricked point from the contour values on the vertical scale. Join the marks with a smooth line to show the profile, and add a river or road where the line crosses it. State the horizontal scale, the vertical scale and the vertical exaggeration beneath the finished figure, and label the start and end points.
questions.explanation: The procedure must be sequential, and the declaration of scales and exaggeration earns a specific part of the marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how a geography project should be planned, conducted and presented.
questions.answer: Planning begins with a clear aim and a hypothesis that can be tested, chosen so that it can be answered by observation within the available time. The method must then be fixed in advance: the location and extent of the study, the dates and times of observation, the instruments used, the number of samples or the length of the transect, and the way each observation will be recorded. Conducting the work means recording data at the moment of observation with units and a note of any unusual condition, keeping raw readings rather than only averages, and repeating readings where error is likely. Presentation follows a fixed structure: title and aim, method, the data in tables exactly as observed, analysis using maps, graphs and simple averages, findings that answer the aim directly, and a limitations section stating what the data cannot show. Every table and figure is numbered and titled, every figure carries units, and any borrowed data is cited with its source. A conclusion that goes beyond the data, or an uncited figure, is what costs most marks.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the aim, method, analysis and limitations all present, since the structure itself is what Paper II assesses.

questions.prompt: During a field study a student measures a 25 mm rainfall, records the river cross-section as 8 cm wide and 40 cm deep, and reports a gradient of 0.5% over a 2 km stretch. Identify any errors in notation or method and state how each should be corrected.
questions.answer: The first entry is ambiguous: rainfall is recorded in millimetres, so 25 mm of rainfall is correct notation only if the units are stated, and it must be written as 25.0 mm with the period of collection given, otherwise a reader cannot tell whether it is a measurement or a count. The second mixes units with the map: a width of 8 cm is meaningless without the map scale, so it should be given as a ground distance converted by the scale, for example 8 cm at 1:50,000 is 4 km, and a depth of 40 cm should be stated in metres as 0.4 m if it is a real measurement, or as 40 mm if it is a scaled drawing measurement. The gradient figure cannot be verified as stated because the vertical drop is missing: a gradient of 0.5 per cent over 2 km means a fall of 10 metres, so that drop should be recorded alongside the distance for the result to be checkable. The corrected record therefore states every quantity with its unit, converts map measurements through the scale, and gives both quantities behind any ratio.
questions.explanation: Marks are for finding all three defects and giving a specific correction for each, since the exercise is about reproducibility rather than arithmetic alone.
